name: Aaron Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fernhill's 250 hectares of grass and maize, with 220 dairy cows. We put in two robot milkers in 2022, so the cows milk themselves when they like, and I check the robot reports on my phone with my first coffee. My day's mostly cows, feed, and fixing whatever broke overnight. My wife Ruth rears the calves, and I use an AI assistant every day for the feed rations, the vet records and the milk contract figures.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like running a tight farm, frankly. Seeing the yield per cow go up and the vet bill go down. What wears me out is the milk price, which is set by people who've never seen a cow, and the rules that change every year. Sundays I'm in church with Ruth, and that's the one day the phone stays in the drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was useful but not magic, and that the farmers who used it still came out ahead. I'd probably say that at the dairy discussion group. I'd not be gloating, just saying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frankly, for me it means more of the same, and the same is good. The robot milkers already paid for themselves, the farm's clear of debt, and we've savings behind us. The milk price is the only real worry, and that's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what we're doing. Keep using the AI for rations and records. I'd keep an eye out for land nearby, because there's always someone retiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the next generation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter Grace is an agronomist, she advises arable farms on crops. The plan is she comes home and takes Fernhill on in a few years. In AI Plateau, nothing changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the milk price. What happens there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milk buyer dropped us three pence a litre last spring with a month's notice. That's the world we're in, AI or no AI. You run tight, you keep cash, you ride it out.

say: Farmers who used it still **came out ahead**.
I'd say it at the **discussion group**, not gloating, just saying.
think: More of the same is **good** for Fernhill.
The **robot milkers** paid for themselves, and we're clear of debt.
do: Keep using AI for **rations and records**.
Keep an eye out for **land nearby** from retiring neighbours.
Keep milking through the two **robot milkers**.
S0.quote: The milk buyer dropped us three pence a litre last spring with a month's notice.
fieldNote: Already **automated**: robot milkers since 2022 and daily AI use.
Treats **milk price swings** as normal business risk.
Has a clear **successor** in his daughter Grace.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant for rations and vet records
Keep milking 220 cows through the two robot milkers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for farmers who are willing to work at it. The market rewards the ones who move. I'd say it at the discussion group and on the dairy forum, and some would think I'm smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's an advantage. The thinking jobs, the rations, the buying, the contract figures, I've already handed half to AI, and I'd hand over the rest. The robots coming slowly into field work suits me, because I'll be ready when they're cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd let AI handle all the feed buying and the milk contract talks, with me checking. I'd put in for the Hartley farm when it comes up, about 60 hectares, because old Hartley's 74 and his son doesn't want it. And I'd take on an apprentice to learn the robots, because skills matter more than any grant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit eager. This is the kind of change I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle round you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some neighbours would struggle, the ones who've never touched a computer. I'd help if they asked, but I'm not going to stop farming well to make my neighbours comfortable. That's not how the market works, and it's not how my father worked either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Grace's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace's job is mostly thinking work, crop plans and reports for clients, so she'd feel it more than me. I'd tell her that's one more reason to come home sooner. Fernhill needs someone who understands both the crops and the computers.

say: This is **good for farmers** willing to work at it.
The market **rewards** the ones who move.
I'd say it on the **dairy forum**, even if some think I'm smug.
think: I've already handed **half the thinking jobs** to AI and would hand over the rest.
**Slow robots** in field work suit me; I'll be ready when they're cheap.
do: Let AI handle **feed buying** and milk contract talks.
Bid for the **Hartley farm**, about 60 hectares, when it comes up.
Take on an **apprentice** to learn the robots.
S1.quote: I'm not going to stop farming well to make my neighbours comfortable.
fieldNote: Sees disruption as **market reward** for those who move first.
Wants an **apprentice**, valuing skills over grants.
Notes his daughter **Grace's** advisory work is more exposed than farming.

steps.text: Hand feed buying and milk contract talks to AI, with checks
Bid for the 60-hectare Hartley farm when it's sold
Take on an apprentice to learn the robot milkers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast, and the people who prepared will be fine. I'd tell farmers not to wait for government to save them. I'd say churches and neighbours should look out for the ones who get hit hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, Fernhill would do well, but I'd be uneasy about the milk price. By 2028 every buyer would have AGI doing the sums, and by 2031 big robot dairies could produce milk cheaper than anyone. Being ahead helps, but if everyone's automated, the price falls for all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd buy a third robot milker and a feed-pushing robot, about 150,000, before the rush. From 2028 I'd let the AI do all the planning and selling. I'd buy land from neighbours who want out, at a fair price, and I'd ask Grace to come home in 2028, not 2031, because her agronomy work would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my own job, but about the price, and about the people round me who wouldn't cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would buying neighbours' land feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frankly, I'd feel a bit like a vulture. But they'd be selling anyway, and I'd rather they sold to a neighbour than to a city investor. I'd pay them properly and let them stay in their houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace would come home, and I'd hand her more than I'd planned, sooner. We'd sit in the kitchen with Ruth and work out a partnership. I'd tell my daughter Grace that the cows don't care whether the farm runs on robots, they care whether someone's paying attention.

say: The people who **prepared** will be fine.
Don't wait for government; **churches and neighbours** should look out for each other.
think: Fernhill would do well, but the **milk price** would fall for everyone.
**Big robot dairies** from 2031 could undercut us all.
do: Buy a **third robot milker** and feed pusher for about 150,000.
Buy **neighbours' land** at a fair price.
feel: **Uneasy** about prices and **neighbours**, not his own job.
S2.quote: The cows don't care whether the farm runs on robots, they care whether someone's paying attention.
fieldNote: Prepared and **well placed**, but sees falling prices as a shared risk.
Admits feeling like **a vulture** buying land from struggling neighbours.
AGI in 2028 pulls his **daughter's homecoming** forward.

steps.text: Buy a third robot milker and a feed pusher for about 150,000
Hand all planning and milk selling to AI from 2028
Bring Grace home in 2028 as a partner in Fernhill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone who wants to be ready. I'd also say families should start talking about who's taking over, because that's where most farms go wrong. That one I'd say at church as much as at the discussion group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me the timing is good. AGI in 2031, robots around 2034, when I'm 66 and Grace has been running things for a few years. I'd be the old man who set it all up and then stepped back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand over day-to-day running to Grace by 2030. I'd put money into robots in stages, a feed pusher first, then field robots once they're proven on bigger farms. And I'd keep buying land when it comes up, steadily, not all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite looking forward to it, frankly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Grace split the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Grace to farm her way, which would probably be more robots than me. I'd keep doing the bit I enjoy, walking the cows in the evening, and stay out of the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the young people round here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want two apprentices on the farm, learning the robots and the cows both. Young people need a trade, and a robot dairy still needs someone who knows when a cow's not right. That's what I'd push for, not handouts.

say: Five years is **plenty** for anyone who wants to be ready.
Families should start talking about **who's taking over**.
think: The timing is **good**: robots around 2034, when I'm 66.
**Grace** would already be running things by then.
do: Invest in **robots in stages**, feed pusher first.
Keep buying **land** steadily as it comes up.
S3.quote: A robot dairy still needs someone who knows when a cow's not right.
fieldNote: The five-year warning matches his **handover plan** neatly.
Favours **apprenticeships** over handouts, a clear traditional thread.
Invests **in stages**, waiting for proof on bigger farms.

steps.text: Hand day-to-day running of Fernhill to Grace by 2030
Buy a feed pusher first, then field robots once proven
Take on two apprentices to learn both robots and cows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and any farmer who wastes it has only himself to blame. I'd say it plainly at the discussion group. Some wouldn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's after I've handed on. AGI comes when I'm 68 and robots when I'm 71. Grace would be running Fernhill, and I'd be in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as now, adding tools as they come. Grace takes over around 2031. I'd help her buy the robots when they're ready, out of the savings, as my part of the handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace when you hand it over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Grace what my father told me. A farm belongs to the family, and each of us just keeps it for a while. Grace would keep it for a while after me, and then her children, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would bother you about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The only thing that would bother me is if the government tried to slow it all down with rules. Let farms adapt at their own pace. The good ones always do.

say: Any farmer who **wastes it** has only himself to blame.
I'd say it **plainly** at the discussion group, though some wouldn't like it.
think: AGI and robots arrive **after I've handed on**.
**Grace** would be running Fernhill, with me in the background.
do: Keep adding **new tools** as they come.
Pay for her **robots** out of savings as his part of the handover.
S4.quote: A farm belongs to the family, and each of us just keeps it for a while.
fieldNote: Sees himself as a **keeper** of the farm for the next generation.
His only worry is **government rules** slowing farms down.
Plans to fund the **robots** as his handover gift to Grace.

steps.text: Keep adding new AI tools at Fernhill as they come out
Pay for Grace's robots from savings as part of the handover

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, but more for my neighbours and the milk price than for Fernhill. What would help is less red tape, so farms can adapt fast, and more apprenticeships, so young people learn the new trades on real farms. Churches and families will look after the rest, like they always have.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we owe each other. I'll do well out of this, most likely, and then it's on me to help the neighbours who don't. I should take on young people who need a start, too.

headlineQuote: I'll do well out of this, most likely, and then it's on me to help the neighbours who don't.
portrait: A 58-year-old **dairy farmer** at Fernhill who uses AI daily and installed robot milkers in 2022.
Believes the **market rewards** farmers who move first, and distrusts government rules.
Values **family, church** and apprenticeships, and plans to hand the farm to his daughter Grace.
Calm in most pictures, **uneasy** in the fastest about milk prices and neighbours.
Admits feeling like **a vulture** when buying land from neighbours who sell up.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mainly for his neighbours and the milk price.
whatWouldHelp: **Less red tape** so farms can adapt fast.
More **apprenticeships** on real farms for young people.
